analysis.one_liner: Raises the corporate tax rate for companies whose CEOs earn over 50 times the median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee never acted on the bill, and it died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise a company's federal corporate tax rate above the standard 21% if it pays its CEO or highest-paid employee more than 50 times what its median worker earns. The surcharge starts at 0.5 percentage points and climbs to 5 points for ratios above 500 to 1. Companies with less than $100 million in average annual gross receipts are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large companies with wide pay gaps, who could see pressure to lift median pay or narrow executive compensation to avoid the tax, plus the public through additional federal revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a surcharge on top of the 21% corporate rate: 0.5 points for pay ratios above 50 to 1, rising in steps to 5 points above 500 to 1 [S2][S3].
The tax is tied to the pay-ratio figures corporations already report to the SEC, using their own disclosed CEO and median-worker compensation [S3].

It also applies to large private companies (at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts) that would otherwise not have to disclose a pay ratio, requiring them to calculate and report one under Treasury rules [S3].
The bill directs Treasury to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio by using contractors instead of employees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with CEO-to-worker pay ratios above 50 to 1, which would owe the surcharge; to the extent they respond by cutting executive pay or raising median wages, shareholders and executives bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies with wide pay gaps

drawbacks.text: The surcharge is modest (0.5 to 5 percentage points), so a company might simply pay the tax rather than change its pay structure, limiting any real effect on wages [S2][S3].
It taxes the gap rather than directly mandating pay, and revenue flows to the Treasury generally rather than to affected workers [S3].
Companies could restructure workforces to shrink the reported ratio; the bill authorizes anti-avoidance rules but effectiveness would depend on Treasury drafting and enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is indirect but real: a recurring tax penalty for very wide pay gaps, with anti-gaming rules, that nudges large firms toward either raising median pay or narrowing executive compensation. The design has genuine limits — the penalty is small enough that many firms may treat it as a cost of doing business, and the burden falls on corporations rather than putting money directly in workers' pockets. On balance it is a targeted, modestly designed lever against a widely reported problem, with no apparent cost to workers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill in the Senate on January 18, 2024, joined by Senators Warren, Van Hollen, and Markey [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which is the last action recorded [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever followed, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with CEO pay far above 50 times their median worker's pay are better off: they avoid any new tax tied to their pay ratios. Committee leadership faces no political cost for never scheduling it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations with wide pay gaps

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act of 2024 and recruited three cosponsors.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on January 18, 2024 and took no further action on it; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all five supporters were Democrats plus independent Bernie Sanders, and no Republicans signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Large corporations with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps
industries.note: They would owe a surcharge of 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of the 21% corporate rate unless they narrowed the pay gap. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs against the bill's goal of lifting median pay relative to executive pay.

industries.industry: Small businesses (under $100 million in gross receipts)
industries.note: They are exempt from the surcharge and from any pay-ratio reporting requirement, avoiding compliance costs their larger competitors would face.
